# Alley Cat: DOS reconstruction and portable C port

This project contains two implementations of Alley Cat (1984): a NASM
reconstruction of the DOS executable and a playable C source port for desktop
and browser use. They share the original game logic and data, but have different
completion criteria.

## Status at a glance

| Source | Current status | What remains |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`src/`](src/README.md) — DOS ASM | Builds the complete 55,067-byte MZ executable from source and passes its pinned SHA-256 and byte-ownership checks. | Further interpretation and annotation of reconstructed code/data as evidence improves. |
| [`portable_src/`](portable_src/README.md) — C port | Playable startup, alley, rooms, rewards, results, audio and controls on SDL3 and WebAssembly. Full parity is unproven. | Execution speed/audio timing, further progression and failure coverage, and physical device/platform acceptance. |

Read the [ASM status and verification contract](docs/SOURCE_OWNERSHIP.md) and
[portable status and remaining work](portable_src/docs/STATUS.md) before using
either source as a reference. Reproducing the DOS bytes does not establish
that the C port reproduces every behavior or its original execution speed.

## Build the DOS reconstruction

Requirements: Python 3, NASM and Make. From the repository root:

```sh
make recon-build
make recon-source-verify
make decomp-coverage
```

Output: `build/recon-layout/RECONCAT.EXE`. The original `CAT.EXE` is not included
and is not required to assemble this output. Verification checks the pinned
hash and source ownership; it does not perform a fresh original-file comparison.
Run the reconstructed executable in a suitable DOS environment.

## Play or build the C port

See the [desktop build instructions](portable_src/README.md#desktop-build),
[browser build instructions](portable_src/README.md#browser-build), and
[controls](portable_src/README.md#controls). Both targets assemble their initial
game data from `src/`; keep the two source directories together.

The browser site runs the C port as WebAssembly. The
[Pages workflow](.github/workflows/pages.yml) builds and deploys that static site
when GitHub Pages is configured to use GitHub Actions.

## Attribution

This is a noncommercial historical reconstruction. Rights in original
game-derived material remain with their holders. The BIOS text font is
attributed to IBM; its source and coverage are documented in the
[font notice](portable_src/assets/fonts/README.md). Asset-specific notices stay
with the corresponding assets. No repository-wide license has been chosen.

justrhoto-anacreon-web-readme-md.text:
# Anacreon: Reconstruction 4021 — Browser Port

A native browser port of the DOS strategy game Anacreon (TMA / George Moromisato; v2.0 by Adam Luker).

The game engine is a faithful hand translation of the original Turbo Pascal source into JavaScript. It covers the economy, fleets, combat, NPE (computer empire) AI, scenarios, news and messages. The DOS text-mode interface has been replaced with a browser-native UI: a zoomable galaxy map, a selection panel with context actions, list tabs and dialogs for every command.

**Play it now:** the port is fully playable in your browser at **https://justrhoto.github.io/anacreon-web/**. You don't need to install anything.

## Running

```
npm install
npm run dev       # development server
npm run build     # static build in dist/ (works from any sub-path)
npm test          # engine simulation and API smoke tests
```

Games are saved in the browser (IndexedDB). You can export saves and import them again, and you can also import custom `.SCN` scenario files.

## Layout

- `src/runtime/`: Pascal semantics (Turbo Pascal RNG, Round, Str/Val, sets), the in-memory file system and CP437 decoding.
- `src/engine/`: the translated game units (PRIMINTR, FLEET, UPDATE, ATTACK, NPE*, NEWGAME, …), plus a UI-free API:
  - `views.js`: read-only views.
  - `commands.js`: player commands.
  - `battle.js`: interactive battles.
  - `game.js`: turn flow, save and load.
- `src/ui/`: the React interface.
- `public/data/`: the original scenarios and help file.

## Deliberate deviations from the original

- Version 11 scenarios (PRINCES.SCN) have an extra reserved field in CREATESTARBASE. The port now skips it; before, the scenario failed to load.
- Auto-attacking a construction site or stargate now actually destroys it. The original only printed the message.
- Dangling-fleet cases that could crash the original (refuel or abort orders aimed at a destroyed fleet) are guarded.

The original DOS source and release files are kept locally in `.dos/` and are not committed.

lardratboy-fallout-decomp-readme-md.text:
# FallOut (1991) — reconstructed C source

`FALLOUT.EXE` is a VGA (320×200, mode 13h) falling-symbols puzzle game for DOS,
written by Brad P. Taylor in 1991. The original source was not available. This
repository holds C source recovered from the executable, plus the tools used to
recover it and to **prove the result behaves identically to the original**.

| | |
|---|---|
| ![menu](docs/menu.png) | ![game](docs/gameplay.png) |
| ![title](docs/title.png) | ![cheat](docs/cheat.png) |

*Screenshots rendered by the reconstructed C code (native test build).*

## What's here

```
FALLOUT.EXE          the original (LZEXE 0.91 packed), untouched
src/fallout.c        the game: 87 functions, in original order, with original offsets
src/gfx.c, gfx.h     C versions of the original's hand-written assembly module
src/data/*.inc       sprites, palette, fonts, tables extracted from the EXE (generated)
tests/*.keys         key scripts used for differential testing
tests/his/           FALLOUT.HIS fixtures for the high-score file tests
tools/               unpacker, analysis scripts, data generator, test harnesses
ports/sdl/           modern port (in progress), built from the unmodified sources
docs/                screenshots and an asset sheet (docs/assets.png)
```

## Building the DOS game

The source targets **Turbo C++ 1.0** (1990), small memory model — the compiler
the original was built with (identified from its C0 startup code and runtime
library). Turbo C++ 1.01 should work too. In DOS (or DOSBox):

```
cd src
tcc -ms fallout.c gfx.c
```

`gfx.c` uses Turbo C pseudo-registers (`_AX`, …) and `geninterrupt()` for the
BIOS/DOS calls, so it is Turbo/Borland C specific. The original was additionally
compressed with LZEXE; that step is optional.

The reconstruction has not been compiled with Turbo C++ yet; see
*Limitations* below.

## How the source was recovered

1. **Unpacking.** `tools/unlzexe.py` decompresses the LZEXE 0.91 image
   (62,170-byte load module, 3 relocations).
2. **Identifying the pieces.** The startup code is Borland's `C0S` (small model),
   followed by three regions:
   * `0x0239–0x43AD` — the C game module (87 functions);
   * `0x43AE–0x5FE3` — a hand-written assembly module (blitters with fully
     unrolled 200-row loops, board match/collapse logic, BIOS/DOS wrappers);
   * `0x5FE4–` — the Turbo C++ runtime library (`rand`, `sprintf`, `delay`,
     `sound`, `system`, long-arithmetic helpers, …).
3. **Decompilation.** Ghidra 12 (headless, `tools/Annotate.java` +
   `tools/annotations.txt`) produced a first draft once it was given the
   library names, the register-argument helpers (`N_LXMUL@` etc.) and overrides
   for Turbo C's sparse `switch` tables (`tools/find_switches.py`). Every
   function was then rewritten by hand against an annotated disassembly
   (`tools/listing.py`). The draft decompiler output was wrong in several
   places, e.g. register tracking in `trans_bands` and dropped `switch` cases.
4. **Data.** Every DGROUP object was located from code and pointer references
   (`tools/dsrefs.py`). `tools/gen_data.py` writes the graphics and tables as C
   initialisers (`src/data/*.inc`); `docs/assets.png` shows them all.
5. **Layout.** Turbo C emits initialised globals where they are defined and a
   function's string literals right after that function, so the order of
   strings and variables in the data segment reveals the original source order.
   `fallout.c` places its definitions to reproduce the original data segment
   offset-for-offset (comments give each object's `DS:` offset). Unreferenced
   variables are kept as `unused_xxxx`.

## Verification: differential emulation

The C code is not trusted on inspection alone. It was **run side by side with the
original binary** and compared frame by frame:

* `tools/emu/run_original.py` runs the *original* unpacked EXE in the Unicorn
  8086 emulator with a small, deterministic BIOS/DOS. Time is "number of BIOS
  tick reads", and keys come from a script.
* `tools/emu/harness.c` compiles the *reconstructed* `fallout.c` + `gfx.c`
  natively against the same model, using a flat 1 MB array for far memory.
* At **every** read of the BIOS clock and every `delay()` call, both write
  the CRC of the whole VGA frame buffer plus score/level/bonus/total to a
  trace. (The end-of-game tally runs on `delay()` alone, without reading the
  clock.) The traces must be identical, including every keypress, every
  `sound()`/`nosound()` call, video-mode change, DOS message and the exit
  code.

Test inputs (`tests/`) include random key fuzzing, scripted play at every
difficulty and start level, menus, cheat mode, pause, the boss key, high-score
entry and saving, quitting from every screen, and start-up failures (no VGA, out
of memory). Three scripts start with a `FALLOUT.HIS` present (`# ENV=HIS_FILE=`,
fixtures from `tests/his/mkhis.py`): a full table and a truncated one, each
loaded, beaten and saved, and one quit without saving. Every byte the game
writes to the file is compared too. They also include several long games played by a bot
(`tools/emu/bot.py`) that steers the original game from its memory; its
keystrokes are recorded and replayed on both sides. The bot games reach
level 200+ and scores in the millions; one (`bot_wrap`, recorded with
`run_original.py --lose-at-level 182`) loses on purpose at level 182 so that
the end-of-game tally wraps the 16-bit bonus.

**Result: all 35 scripts produce identical traces — about 1,050,000 frames
at clock reads plus 125,000 at `delay()` calls and 255,000 speaker calls
compared, with zero differences.** Source-line coverage of `fallout.c` over the
suite is 98.4%. The lines not reached are `break`s after `exit()`, code the
original can never execute, and the "slow machine" and midnight-wraparound
guards, which a deterministic clock cannot trigger.

To run it yourself (needs `pip install unicorn`, a C compiler and zlib;
set `PYTHON=` to use a virtualenv's interpreter):

```
tools/emu/run_all.sh                 # every script, prints MATCH/DIFFER
tools/emu/difftest.sh tests/fuzz1.keys
tools/emu/coverage.sh tests/*.keys   # clang source coverage
```

The native build compiles a copy of `fallout.c` derived by
`tools/emu/mkport.py`, and the SDL port uses the same copy:

* The uninitialised globals are packed into one struct in their original order
  (`tools/emu/mkbss.py`). The original reads past the end of `board[]` in one
  case (see below), and this keeps those reads hitting the same neighbouring
  data.
* Three expressions are patched to wrap at 16 bits as Turbo C's `int` does.
  The one that matters in play is `bonus`: the end-of-game tally adds up to
  1000 per level, so at high levels the original's bonus wraps past 65535
  (`tests/bot_wrap.keys`). `MKPORT_FLAGS=--no-int16` builds without the
  patches.
* `struct hiscore` is packed into its DOS layout (8-byte name, 32-bit score,
  16-bit slot), so the table in memory is the 140-byte `FALLOUT.HIS`, as on
  DOS. A name with no NUL is drawn on into its score bytes, as the original
  does (`tests/t_his_load.keys`).

## Things the original does that you might not expect

These are reproduced faithfully in the source and commented there.

* **Off-board read when rotating.** Rotating a horizontal piece on the bottom
  row tests `board[17][col]`, one row past the array. That byte is
  `shell_cmd[4]`, the `E` of the default boss-key command `PAUSE`, so the
  rotation is refused. With a boss-key command of four characters or fewer,
  the piece would rotate off the board.
* **Bomb placement** tries nine random columns and keeps the last. The bomb is
  armed if *any* try landed below row 5. Columns are chosen with
  `rand() * 6 / 32767`, so bombs only ever appear in the left six columns. A bomb spawns on about 1 in 200
  pieces, or 1 in 10 in cheat mode. Kind 0 gives you an extra bomb; kind 1
  detonates at once for +500.
* **A bomb** removes every symbol of the most common kind on the board.
* **Difficulty menu:** after a choice, the highlight is moved 20 pixels too low.
  It is redrawn immediately afterwards, so this is barely visible.
* `draw_panel()` takes five parameters, but every caller passes a sixth (a
  colour) that it ignores. No prototype was in scope.
* The level menu has no starting level 2 (`3` starts level 3), so the
  "level 2 → 1 bomb" branch can never run.
* `get_pixel()` returns a 16-bit word, so title-screen stars are drawn only
  where *two* adjacent pixels are black. `copy_rect()` copies whole words.
* Assembly routines that are never called: a "recolour" fill that clobbers `BP`
  and compares each pixel with itself, plus hardware-scroll and split-screen
  helpers. `set_small_color2()` is never called either.
* `vga_present()` calls INT 10h/1A00h, ignores the result, and returns the
  BIOS byte at `0040:008A` instead.
* Undocumented keys:
  * `A` in game abandons the current game.
  * `V` increments a variable that nothing reads.
  * `F1` on the title screen adds stars.
  * `B` in the difficulty menu turns on **cheat mode**, which makes bombs
    frequent and disables high scores.
* `FALLOUT.HIS` is the 140-byte high-score table XORed with 2, 4, 6, …
  (a byte, so the key wraps after 127 bytes). It is saved only when quitting
  with `Q` from the main menu; F10 never saves. A short file leaves the rest of
  the default table in memory, and that gets scrambled along with the file.
* Score arithmetic is 16-bit (`n * multiplier / 2`), as in the original, and
  so is `bonus`: a game ending at a high enough level wraps it during the
  end-of-game tally, losing 65536 points.

## Limitations / possible next steps

* **Not yet compiled with Turbo C++.** The goal was behavioural equivalence,
  which is what the tests prove. Rebuilding with Turbo C++ 1.0/1.01 in DOSBox
  would be the next check, both that it compiles and how close the machine code
  is. Exact matches would also need the original's local-variable declaration
  order and similar details.
* The assembly module is provided as C. Its behaviour is preserved, but its
  unrolled-loop speed is not.
* A modern SDL port is in `ports/sdl/` (see its README): playable, with sound
  and high scores. It compiles the unmodified sources against a DOS stand-in
  layer, and its replay mode is checked against the original's traces.

zapolnov-superplex3d-prototype-readme-md.text:
This repository contains a C++ code of a Supaplex clone. It has a
brand new 3D art, but its game logic was recovered from an original
Supaplex executable via disassembly.

**Please read the Legal Information at the end of this document.
It contains important notices about the legal state of this code.**

The game is by no means complete. It does not have any menu or UI.
By default game starts in the first level. To choose a level, please
create a `level.cfg` file with a level number in the directory of
the executable file.

Building
========

Please use CMake (http://www.cmake.org/) to build the project.

I have tested build in the following environments:

  * Apple OSX Yosemite with Xcode 6.1.1.
  * Ubuntu Linux 14.10 with GCC 4.9.1.
  * Ubuntu Linux 14.10 with MinGW-w64 4.9.1 (cross-compile to Windows).

If you are using another system or compiler, your mileage may vary. Anyway,
the code is quite portable so it should build and run with very little efforts.
Feel free to contact me via e-mail zapolnov@gmail.com if you have any
problems.

On Ubuntu Linux you may use the following command to install required packages
before building:

    sudo apt-get install \
        build-essential \
        cmake \
        libgl1-mesa-dev \
        libglu1-mesa-dev \
        libx11-dev \
        libxrandr-dev \
        libxcursor-dev \
        libxi-dev \
        libxinerama-dev \
        libxxf86vm-dev

I have also provided Win32 and OSX Yosemite binaries in the `bin` directory for
your convenience.

Engine
======

The code uses 3D engine I was writing at that time. Originally engine code used
the Qt library. Later I have decided to make it more lightweight and have replaced
Qt classes with self-written implementations (you may find them in the
`engine/core/trolltech.h` file).

At the time when I was writing the engine, GLSL shaders were not
available on all platforms. So, I have included the GLSL compiler from
the Mesa library which compiles them to the ARB assembly and then
passes it to the OpenGL library.

Game logic
==========

All the reverse engineered game logic is in the `supaplex_game.cpp` file.
I have tried to keep it as close to the original, as possible.
The code is far from ideal: it has `goto`s, crypting variable names like
`byte_403C3` and all that stuff. But it is of very good quality for a disassembly.

In the `disassembly` directory you will find some scripts and tools I have used
to disassemble the Supaplex executable.

The `disassembly/decomp.c` file contains a decompressor
for the original, compressed executable - it is very interesting as it contains
(an incomplete) 8086 CPU emulator which runs decompressor instruction-by-instruction,
until a final decompressed executable is produced, then dumps it into a file.

The `disassembly/supaplex.idc` is a script for the Interactive Disassembler Pro
(https://www.hex-rays.com/products/ida/index.shtml). It sets human-readable
names for some symbols and adds useful comments to the code.

The `diassembly/supaplex_debugger.asm` was used to debug the Supaplex code. It
runs the original Supaplex executable and reports when various positions in the
code are hit. I don't remember exactly, but I believe that I have used this tool
to clarify purpose of some parts of the code.

The `disassembly/refactor` subdirectory contains an intermediate C++ code
I have built during the disassembly.

During the original disassembly process I have used a subversion repository.
I have preserved an original history using the svn-to-git import. Feel free to
navigate through history to see how the disassembly evolved (use the "follow
renames" option if you don't see the full history).

Legal information
=================

Artwork
-------

3D models and textures were created by the great guy Andrey Chuloshnikov
(http://growlart.daportfolio.com/, 4growl@gmail.com) as a freelance
job. He was paid for this job and copyright is owned by me (I have all the
necessary legal documents).

So all the models and textures are
Copyright (c) 2009-2014 Nikolay Zapolnov (zapolnov@gmail.com).
Feel free to use them under the terms of the
Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 License
(http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/)

Engine code
-----------

Most of the engine code (everything in the `engine` subdirectory,
except contents of the `3rdparty` directory and some other files)
was written by me and was Copyright (c) 2009 Nikolay Zapolnov.

I hereby release all **my** code in this repository to the public domain.
Feel free to use it for any purpose. Should you need a more legalese
document, please use this one: https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0

3rdparty libraries, sounds and other stuff that was not created (and are not owned)
by me are still copyrighted by their authors and are distributed under the
corresponding licenses. Please see comments at the top of source files for more
information.

Supaplex game logic
-------------------

**I believe, that you are not allowed to use the provided Supaplex game logic code
and disassembly scripts in any way, be that a commercial, free or
open-source project. Probably you are even not allowed to download and/or read
those files.**

Unfortunately, I didn't find a way to contact the original copyright
holder (the Digital Integration company) for a permission. But Maarten Egmond
did contact them long time ago and have received permission to redistribute
the original Supaplex for free (see http://www.elmerproductions.com/sp/faq.html#q_license
for more information). This fact, and also the fact that there are already a
lot of Supaplex clones available in the wild, makes me believe that I am not
doing nothing bad for nobody.

**If you are a copyright holder for the Supaplex and you believe that I infringe
your rights, please contact me immediately via e-mail zapolnov@gmail.com.**

Sounds
------

Sounds and music were downloaded for free from the Internet (via Google).
I do not own any copyright for them.

sirl0ll0-amiga-m68k-decomp-readme-md.text:
# amiga-m68k-decomp

Toolchain e pipeline per la **decompilazione matching di giochi Amiga (M68k)**,
con progress tracking compatibile con [decomp.dev](https://github.com/encounter/decomp.dev).

```
gioco.exe (Hunk) ── make split ──▶ orig/*.bin ──┐
                                                 │  make analyze (Ghidra headless)
                                                 │  make units   (funzioni -> unit)
                 src/*.c, asm/*.s ── vbcc/vasm ─▶ build/*.o ── make report ─▶ build/report.json
```

`build/report.json` usa lo stesso formato di `objdiff` (`REPORT_VERSION = 2`),
quindi puo' alimentare decomp.dev. Nota: **objdiff non supporta M68k**
(solo arm/arm64/mips/ppc/superh/x86): il matching e' fatto da
`tools/diff_m68k.py`. Dettagli in [ARCHITETTURA.md](ARCHITETTURA.md).

## Requisiti

| Cosa | Dove serve | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Python 3 + `pip install -r tools/requirements.txt` | ovunque | capstone per il fuzzy matching |
| Ghidra + estensione `ghidra-amiga` | solo locale | `make analyze` (mai in CI) |
| vbcc nativo **oppure** Docker | build/matching reale | vedi sotto |
| gcc host | solo `make verify` | test layout header |

## Toolchain vbcc (due strade, stesso `+aos68k`)

**A. Nativa Windows — pronta subito, niente reboot.**
Binari ufficiali multi-target (vbccm68k, vc, vasmm68k_mot, vlink + target
`m68k-amigaos` con config `aos68k`):

```powershell
# una tantum: scarica http://www.ibaug.de/vbcc/vbcc_win_x64.zip (16 MB)
# ed estrailo in .toolchain/vbcc-win  (su questa macchina: gia' fatto)
. .\tools\env.ps1
vc +aos68k -c -Iinclude src/main.c -o build/main.o
```

Agent con vbcc reale (va lanciato dalla root: `-Iinclude` è relativo):

```powershell
python tools/agent/loop.py --config tools/agent/config.native-win.json --units config/units.json
```

**B. Docker (CI + Linux).** Richiede `wsl --install` + reboot + Docker Desktop,
poi `make docker-build` e `make report` nel container. Il Dockerfile compila
vbcc dai sorgenti ufficiali (`ibaug.de/vbcc/vbcc.tar.gz`).

## Quickstart (senza gioco: verifica i tool)

```sh
make verify
```

## Uso con un gioco

```sh
# 1. split dell'eseguibile (una tantum)
make split EXE=/path/gioco.exe BASE=0x0

# 2. analisi Ghidra headless (locale; GHIDRA_PROJDIR deve esistere)
make analyze GHIDRA_DIR="/path/Ghidra" EXE=orig/hunk0_CODE.bin

# 3. funzioni -> unit di matching + header LVO
make units

# 4. C di partenza dal decompilatore (locale, opzionale)
make decompile GHIDRA_DIR="/path/Ghidra" GHIDRA_PROG=game.bin

# 5. scrivi src/<funzione>.c o lancia l'agent automatico, poi:
make agent    # varianti -> compile -> diff, tiene il meglio
make report   # in Docker: toolchain Amiga reale
```

## Struttura

- `docker/` — vbcc + vasm + vlink + target m68k-amiga
- `tools/split_hunk.py` — parser Hunk -> `orig/`
- `tools/ghidra/AnalyzeAmiga.java` — export funzioni/simboli/LVO da Ghidra
- `tools/ghidra/amiga_data.json` — mappa memoria, registri custom, LVO Exec (verificati vs NDK)

- `tools/diff_m68k.py` — matching -> `build/report.json` (formato decomp.dev v2)
- `include/amiga_hardware.h` — registri custom (offset verificati)

- [ ] **cpcxray developer notes** (write the instructions for the developer, with the why):
  - Access map: under CP/M the VDOS ROM is always paged in. Data reads of ROM 5 by code

    sjasmplus refuses (`xmon_mnemonics` after the ED test; worked around with one comment per

---

## 3. Bugfix proposals

Patches for bugs found during the analysis - to try later on a copy of the ROM (never change
`roms/`). Each one: where, why, the patch (decoded value and the byte in the scrambled ROM file),
and the test that shows it works. The place is also marked in the source with a comment block
starting `*** BUGFIX PROPOSAL`.

- [ ] **XMON L: RST &28 (FIRM JUMP) ignores its inline word.**
  - Bug: on the CPC, RST 1 (&08 LOW JUMP), RST 2 (&10 SIDE CALL), RST 3 (&18 FAR CALL) and
    RST 5 (&28 FIRM JUMP) are followed by a 2-byte inline word. XMON's table
    `xmon_opcodes_c0` gives RST 1-3 length 3 (byte 0 = &A6), but RST 5 length 1 (byte 0 =
    &26). So `EF 34 12` lists as `RST 28`, `INC (HL)`, `LD (DE),A` instead of one 3-byte
    instruction (observed 2026-10-26, `output/xmon_l/base_opcodes.bin`).
  - Where: only the table byte. No code tests the RST number - `xll_table` (&F114: bits 7-6
    of byte 0 = length - 1) and `xll_byte_loop` / &F15C (next address = after the length)
    treat every RST alike.
  - Patch: **&F5F1 &26 -> &A6** (entry &EF, byte 0); in the scrambled ROM file **offset &35F1:
    &2E -> &AE** (computed with the vortex decoder; &AE is the only raw value giving &A6).
    Result: `EF3412    RST  28`, like `CF3412    RST  08`.
  - Optional second patch (not tried): show the inline word as an operand - byte 2 of the
    entries &FF (none) -> &FE (nn): RST 1 &F593 (raw &F7 -> &F6), RST 2 &F5AB (raw &FF -> &FE),
    RST 3 &F5C3 (raw &FF -> &FE), RST 5 &F5F3 (raw &F7 -> &F6). Expected `RST 28,&1234`
    (path &F2D7-&F2EB as for `JP nn`); side effect: &FE also sets `xmon_branch_target`.
  - Test: a patched copy under `output/` in a test machine (config/machine.toml stays
    unchanged), `L` over `base_opcodes.bin` at &4000.

- [ ] **XMON L: `OUT (n),A` / `IN A,(n)` always show `(&F4)`.**
  - Bug: operand code &F9 = "(n)" (used only by the entries &D3 and &DB) jumps at &F2D2
    (`jr z,xlo_port`) straight to the output, without reading the port byte; H still holds &F4,
    the high byte of the name table pointer (observed: `D3 56` -> `OUT (&F4),A`). Code &FA does
    the same output correctly (reads H = n first) but no table entry uses it.
  - Patch (1 byte, no new space needed): **&F2D3 &57 -> &02** - the jr then goes to &F2D6
    (`ld hl,(xmon_list_address)`), reads the last two instruction bytes like &FA-&FE, and the
    `inc a` chain (&F9 -> &FA, &FB, &FC, &FD at &F30B, not zero) ends in `xlo_port` with H = n.
    In the scrambled ROM file **offset &32D3: &5F -> &0A** (operand byte, decoded; &0A is the
    only raw value giving &02). From reading the code only; not tried.
  - Alternative (2 bytes, table only): operand code &F9 -> &FA in the entries &D3 (&F59E, raw
    &D1 -> &D2) and &DB (&F5B7, raw &D1 -> &D2).
  - Test: `L` over `D3 56` / `DB 56`: expected `OUT (&56),A` / `IN A,(&56)`.
- [ ] **XMON O: ESC in an input leaves the output file open.**
  - Bug (observed 2026-10-26): `xmon_input_word` ends the command on ESC with `jp
    xmon_command_done`; O (&F011) has opened the file with CAS OUT OPEN before its three inputs,
    so ESC leaves it open (`XE.$$$` in the directory). The next O fails silently (file already
    open) and only frees the channel through `xco_abandon`; the third O works. The `.$$$` entry
    stays on the disc.
  - Patch idea: call CAS_OUT_ABANDON before CAS OUT OPEN (3 bytes) - or read the three values
    first and open the file afterwards (reorder &F017-&F032; the name must survive in &ACA5 and
    the values on the stack). No free byte found in O; the reorder needs no new space but HL /
    DE / B of the name must be set up again before CAS OUT OPEN - still to work out. First
    check that CAS_OUT_ABANDON with no file open is harmless in VDOS (not checked).
  - Test: `OB:XE.BIN` + ESC, then `OB:XF.BIN,4000,0032,4000` must write XF.BIN at once.

- [ ] **XMON @: T and G keep an invalid position after `>>`.**
  - Bug (observed 2026-10-26): `xdm_cmd_track` stores the track at &EB65 and `xdm_cmd_block` T / S
    at &EC8C / &EC91 before `xdm_check_block`; on `>>` the position past the last block stays set,
    and the next R / W / D uses it (observed: TA0 `>>`, then R -> `E:45`). A W there could write
    beyond the CP/M area. The manual says an input error changes nothing.
  - Patch idea: check first, then store - e.g. T: keep the old track (`push af` of sek_track) and
    put it back on the error path, or compute the check from A before `ld (sek_track),a`. Needs a
    few more bytes; candidate space: **&ED12-&ED1F (14 bytes, raw 00 = 14 NOPs - run on purpose, no
    reference found)** - also a candidate for the O patch (3 bytes) above. Still to work out.
  - Test: TA0 -> `>>` and T unchanged; GB1 -> `>>` and T / S unchanged.

- [ ] **|GET never reports "Record leer" (set_file_write_flag keeps Z).**
  - Bug (observed 2026-10-26): DR's setfwf uses ORI, which clears Z; VDOS's `set 7,(hl)` at
    &E10B keeps it, so after random_seek's error exit (&E678 `jp set_file_write_flag`)
    read_random_body (&E5ED `call z,sub_e4c2`) reads anyway and the code &FF becomes 1: a record
    in a missing extent reads as empty instead of "Record leer" (msg &37).
  - Patch idea (uses the free bytes): &E678 `jp &ED12` instead of `jp &E108`; at &ED12:
    `call &E0F9` (get_module) / `ld a,(hl)` / `or #80` / `ld (hl),a` / `ret` (8 of the 14 NOPs).
    Only the error exit changes. Opcodes raw, operands scrambled - the raw bytes still to be
    computed with the vortex encoder. Not tried.
  - Test: the simulation scenario without the hand-made Z: |GET,1,2000 -> "Record leer".

- [ ] **CAT shows up to 2K too much free space** (4.5b): `dir_print_free` tests bits 7, 0, 1 of
  the last ALV byte; bits 0 / 1 (no blocks there) count as free. Patch still to work out - first
  check whether it fits in place.
- [ ] **CAT shows file sizes over 512K modulo 512K** (4.5b): `dir_compare_names` / the size
  loop use the extent byte only, not the module byte S2. Patch still to work out; probably needs
  more code than fits in place.

- [ ] **XMON L: ED &8B is shown as `OTDR`.**
  - Bug: `xll_ed_high` (&F1C5) starts with `cp #8B` / `ld a,#45` (OTDR). ED &8B is no Z80
    instruction; OTDR is ED &BB, which the block formula already gives (observed: both ED 8B and
    ED BB show `OTDR`).
  - Patch (1 byte, in place): **&F1C6 &8B -> &00** - A is &7C or more here, so the compare never
    matches and ED &8B falls through to "-??-". In the scrambled ROM file **offset &31C6:
    &AB -> &20** (operand byte; &20 is the only raw value giving &00). From reading the code
    only; not tried.
  - Test: `L` over `ED 8B` / `ED BB`: expected `-??-` / `OTDR`.

- [ ] **XMON L: DD / FD display weaknesses** (observed 2026-10-26, doc 3.5.18). No patch worked
  out yet; most need more code than fits in place:
  1. invalid `DD xx` / `FD xx` (and `DD CB d` + odd op) shown as 3 bytes, one too many:
     `xll_index_op` (&F25F) jumps to `xll_invalid` (length 2), and `xll_show` (&F13D) adds 1 for
     the prefix. Better: show the prefix alone (1 byte) and go on with xx.
  2. `DD CB d 36` (SLL) shown as `SRL`: &F228 `cp #07 / jr nz / dec a` maps 7 to 6, so 6 and 7
     both give mnemonic &10. Better: y = 6 -> "-??-" (as the CB branch does at &F0ED).
  3. undocumented `DD CB d op` with a register (low bits <> 6) shown as the plain (IX+d) form:
     only bit 0 is checked at &F219. Better: low bits <> 6 -> "-??-".
  4. displacement shown unsigned (`(IX+&FD)` for -3); cosmetic.

- [ ] **XMON R switches the printer echo off.**
  - Bug: `xmon_edit_word` (&F9D6) shows each value with `xmon_hex_byte_quiet` twice and never puts
    the switch back (&BEFE -> &BEFF); the second call saves the cleared switch. Observed: P on,
    R, RETURN -> &BEFE / &BEFF 01 01 -> 00 00.
  - Patch (2 bytes, in place): call `xmon_hex_byte` (&FA28) instead of `xmon_hex_byte_quiet`
    (&FA1B) at &F9DF and &F9E3: **&F9E0 &1B -> &28** (raw offset **&39E0: &1B -> &28**) and
    **&F9E4 &1B -> &28** (raw offset **&39E4: &3B -> &08**). The switch is then never touched,
    and the printer gets the final value of each register. Not tried.
  - Test: P on, R, a few RETURNs: &BEFF stays 01.

- [ ] **XMON A destroys XMON's copy of the user's RAM &0080-&0094.**
  - Bug: `xmon_input_line` (&EE3F) fills its buffer &ACA5-&ADA3 (C = 255 from A) with spaces and
    puts the text there; XMON's low-RAM copy (`xmon_save_low_ram`, &AD76-&AD8A) lies inside it.
    The next read from &8000 on writes spaces / text into &0080-&0094 (observed: `A9000,Z`,
    `D8000,8001` -> 21 spaces at &0080). Under CP/M &0080 is the command line / DMA buffer.
  - Patch (1 byte, in place): A's maximum **&FCD2 &FF -> &D1** (209 characters; the buffer then
    ends at &AD75, just below the copy); raw offset **&3CD2: &F7 -> &D9**. Only A calls
    `xmon_input_line`, so nothing else changes. Not tried. (Moving the copy would keep 255
    characters but needs more changes.)
  - Test: `A9000,Z`, `D8000,8001`: &0080-&0094 unchanged.

- [ ] **XMON T: bugs of the single step** (all observed 2026-10-26, doc 3.5.18).
  1. After a done RET (`xtr_ret` &F82A) the step count becomes the return address and the next
     listing starts at the user SP - T runs away and can lose control. Patch (1 byte, in place):
     **&F839 &31 -> &2A** (jp &F92A instead of jp &F931; raw offset **&3839: &39 -> &22**) - HL = PC
     and DE = the count are loaded again (the RET step itself is then not counted). Not tried.
  2. RET cc is always taken (`xtr_ret` does not test the condition). Needs code (test the
     condition against the user F) - no patch yet.
  3. RST &00 / &20 / &30 / &38 are done like a RET (&F826 falls into `xtr_ret`). Better: treat
     them as "next instruction" (RST 4 RAM LAM returns there). No patch yet.
  4. RST &08 / &28: `POP HL` at &F86F without a `PUSH HL` (&F804 -> &F860). A word from XMON's
     stack becomes the "next" address, F7 is written there, XMON's SP moves. No patch yet (needs
     a PUSH HL on that path).
  5. A jump to itself (DJNZ $ / JR $) never runs; 6. after RST &10 / &18 the code to the caller
     runs unstepped - design weaknesses.

- [ ] **XMON M: an overlapping copy upwards lands one byte too high.**
  - Bug: `xcm_backward` (&F786) sets DE = target + length (the `INC BC` at &F78E comes before the
    `ADD HL,BC`), one too high. Observed: `M4000,4003,4002` on `11 22 33 44 55 66 77` ->
    `11 22 33 11 22 33 44` instead of `11 22 11 22 33 44 77`.
  - Patch (5 bytes, in place, no new space): reorder &F78E-&F792 `03 E1 EB 09 EB` ->
    `E1 EB 09 EB 03` (ld b,h / ld c,l / pop hl / ex de,hl / add hl,bc / ex de,hl / inc bc); the
    same bytes at file offset &378E-&3792 (opcodes are stored unscrambled). Not tried.
  - Test: `M4000,4003,4002` -> `11 22 11 22 33 44 77`.
- [ ] **XMON M: an end below the start copies nearly 64K** (read, not tried) - a guard
  (`jr c` to the prompt after the length) needs a few bytes.

Space for patches that do not fit in place: &ED12-&ED1F (14 NOPs, no reference) and &FFC0-&FFFF
(64 bytes, `rom_tail_copy`: a fully scrambled duplicate of &FF40-&FF7F that nothing reaches or
copies - checked 2026-10-26, safe to overwrite).

# Nibby Nibble — emulated Java port

[Version française](README.fr.md) · [Native version (repository root)](../README.md)

Java port of the Amiga game **Nibby Nibble** (© 1993 Gabriele Roncolato, presented by Amiga News),
obtained by decompiling the original 68000 program (`data/Nibby` from the WHDLoad install, kept in `original-assets/Nibby`).

This is the first step of the project: the original routines translated one by one, running on a small
emulation of the Amiga chipset. The [native version](../README.md) at the root of the repository was then
written from this work, and was checked to produce pixel-identical frames against it.

## Screenshots

Frames produced by the Java port (`--headless` mode), scaled ×2.

| | |
|:---:|:---:|
| ![Title screen](docs/screenshots/title.png) | ![Playing level 1](docs/screenshots/level1.png) |
| Title screen | Level 1: the snake has eaten some of the dots |
| ![Level 3](docs/screenshots/level3.png) | ![Death](docs/screenshots/death.png) |
| Level 3 | Death (time out): the body burns from the tail to the head |
| ![End of level](docs/screenshots/fade.png) | ![STAGE screen](docs/screenshots/stage.png) |
| End of level: fade to white | "STAGE" screen shown before each level |

## Preservation and educational purpose

The sole purpose of this project is the **preservation of Amiga video game heritage** and
**educational use**: documenting the inner workings of a 1993 game (68000 code, copper, blitter,
hardware sprites, Paula), showing a complete reverse-engineering process, and keeping the game playable
on today's machines without an emulator.

- The original game, © 1993 Gabriele Roncolato, was distributed as **public domain** software on the
  cover disk of the French magazine *Amiga Dream*. All credit for the game goes to its author.
- The original data file (`data/Nibby` from the WHDLoad install, RNC packed, unmodified) is kept in
  `original-assets/` for preservation. It is not covered by the MIT license.
- This project is strictly non-commercial. If a rights holder wishes it to be taken down, just open an
  issue or contact the author: it will be removed promptly.

Port author: Guillaume Monet (guillaume.monet@free.fr).

### License

The Java code, Python tools and documentation in this repository are under the [MIT](../LICENSE) license.
The original game (public domain, *Amiga Dream* cover disk) remains credited to Gabriele Roncolato; the
disassemblies in `reverse/listings/` are provided for preservation and teaching purposes.

## The port

The game is **not** a loose remake: every routine of the 68000 program was translated into a Java
method (the original address is given in a comment). The resources (graphics, copper lists, levels,
music module) are read directly from the original data file, kept as is in `original-assets/Nibby`:
nothing is extracted or converted.

## Running

Requirement: JDK 21. From the `emu/` folder:

```sh
gradle run
# or
gradle jar
java -jar build/libs/nibbynibble-emu.jar            # looks for original-assets/Nibby
java -jar build/libs/nibbynibble-emu.jar path/to/Nibby
```

Windows builds of this emulated version (Java runtime included) are the releases
[v1.0.0 and v1.0.1](https://github.com/guillaumemonet/nibbynibble-java/releases). To rebuild one:
`gradle jpackageImage` (output in `build/dist/NibbyNibble`).

Options:

| option            | effect                                                         |
|-------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|
| `--scale N`       | window zoom factor (default 3)                                 |
| `--lives`         | "Unlimited Lives" trainer from the WHDLoad install             |
| `--time`          | "Unlimited Time" trainer                                       |
| `--headless N DIR evt...` | runs N frames without a window, saves PNGs and `audio.wav` (testing) |

Headless example: `--headless 700 out 100:fire+ 110:fire- 200:fire+ 205:fire- 320:right+ 400:shot`
(`frame:action` events; actions are `fire|up|down|left|right|lmb|rmb` followed by `+`/`-`,
an Amiga raw key code in hex, or `shot`).

## Controls

| Amiga                      | PC                                  |
|----------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| joystick                   | arrow keys (or numpad 8/2/4/6)      |
| fire button                | Shift, Ctrl or Enter                |
| ESC (back to title)        | Esc                                 |
| quit (F10 under WHDLoad)   | F10 or close the window             |
| right click + fire + left click | same with the mouse: skips the level (original cheat) |

Original cheat: type `THE RONCLER GANG` on the title screen → infinite lives (and the timer stops).

## Rules (derived from the code)

- 20×14 maze of 16×16 tiles; 10 levels that loop (level 11 is level 1 again).
- Eat all the dots before the timer runs out. Each dot is worth 1 (displayed ×10).
- The snake grows by one segment every 2 then 1 dots, alternately (91 segments maximum).
- Walls do not kill: the snake just stops. You can only turn at right angles, on a tile.
- You die by biting yourself (hardware collision between the head sprite and the body playfield),
  or by moving while the timer is at 0. The level then restarts (dots come back, the score is kept).
  You start with 3 spare lives.

## Architecture

```
nibby/Main.java              launcher, Swing window, 50 Hz loop paced by audio, headless mode
nibby/amiga/Rnc.java         Rob Northen ProPack (method 1) decompressor — data/Nibby is packed
nibby/amiga/Memory.java      512 KB of chip RAM; the program image is loaded at $30000
nibby/amiga/Custom.java      $DFFxxx registers (written by the game and by the copper)
nibby/amiga/Video.java       copper + bitplanes (dual playfield) + (attached) sprites + CLXDAT → 320×264 framebuffer
nibby/amiga/Blitter.java     blitter (A/B/C/D channels, shifts, masks, minterms)
nibby/amiga/Paula.java       4 DMA audio voices with the register "latch" behaviour
nibby/amiga/Machine.java     synchronisation: the ported 68000 program runs in its own thread
                             and waits for the VBL just as the original waited for the beam
nibby/game/NibbyNibble.java  the game: title, levels, movement, growth, death, fades, HUD
nibby/game/Replay.java       the original music routine (NoiseTracker style) + sound effects on voice 2
```

Rather than redrawing the screen with Java2D primitives, the port keeps the original display model:
the game writes into copper lists and sprite control words, and has the body drawn by the blitter
through a copper list generated every frame. A small chipset emulation (line-by-line copper, blitter,
sprites, collision detection) is then enough to faithfully render the copper gradients, the dual
playfield and the pixel-accurate collisions that the "bite your own tail" rule depends on.

## Analysis of the original binary

### Loading (`NibbyNibble.slave`, see `reverse/listings/whdload_slave.s`)

The WHDLoad slave loads `data/Nibby` unpacked (RNC) at `$30000`, applies patches (blitter waits,
keyboard: arrows + right Shift, interrupts) then jumps to `$30000`.
Trainers: NOP of `subi #1,$31896` (lives) and of `subi #1,$31898` (time).

### Memory map (256 KB image loaded at `$30000`)

| address           | content                                                                    |
|-------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `$30000-$31818`   | game code                                                                  |
| `$3181A`          | keyboard interrupt (raw code → `$3188A`)                                   |
| `$31878`          | cheat sequence (`THE RONCLER GANG`, raw key codes)                         |
| `$3188A-$31912`   | variables (see the fields of `NibbyNibble`)                                |
| `$31956`          | game copper list (dual playfield 3+2 planes, sprites, palette)            |
| `$31A76`          | death copper list                                                          |
| `$31BFA` / `$31C66` | "STAGE nn" / "GAME OVER" screens                                         |
| `$31CD2`          | status bar copper list                                                     |
| `$31D6E`          | title copper list (180 lines of gradient on COLOR14)                       |
| `$323D2`          | rainbow colour table                                                       |
| `$32484-$33304`   | head sprites (4 directions × 3 frames, attached pairs), tail sprites       |
| `$32FC4-$33784`   | body shapes (32×16, 2 planes), mask, explosion frames                      |
| `$33B04`          | empty tile; `$33B64` working copy of the level                             |
| `$33C7C-$34B90`   | 10 levels: descriptor {map, wall tile, dot tile, palette}, map = dot count, time, 20×14 characters (`0` wall, `.` dot) |
| `$34CBC/$34DFC/$35214` | X shift/offset and Y offset tables for the blitter                    |
| `$35194`          | 8×8 digit font                                                             |
| `$35418-$366D8`   | circular position history (600 entries, mirrored for reading)              |
| `$366D8-$36F66`   | music replay + CIA interrupts                                              |
| `$38000`          | title picture (4 planes 320×200)                                           |
| `$40000`          | ProTracker module "nib-rsi" (sample 16 "esplosione", 17 "bopp")            |
| `$57800`          | status bar (3 planes 320×37)                                               |
| `$5E000/$5F000`   | body blit copper lists (double buffered, generated)                        |
| `$60000/$65000/$6A000` | 3 body playfield buffers (triple buffering)                           |
| `$70000`          | maze playfield (3 interleaved planes)                                      |

### Tools (`reverse/tools`)

Python scripts used for the analysis (Python 3 + `capstone` + `pillow`):

- `rnc.py original-assets/Nibby nibby.bin` — decompression (256 KB image loaded at `$30000`);
- `m68kdis.py nibby.bin start end base` — linear 68000 disassembly (e.g. `0 0x3b64 0x30000`);
- `copper.py nibby.bin address [n]` — copper list decoding.

The extraction of all the graphics, levels and music is done by
[`tools/extract_assets.py`](../tools/extract_assets.py) of the native version.

The disassembly listings are in `reverse/listings`.

## Known differences

- The Amiga low-pass filter (E0x command) is not emulated; the audio output is a direct stereo mix of
  the 4 voices, with a slight crossfeed.
- Timing is per frame (50 Hz): raster waits and blits are instantaneous.

tambourinereindeer-open-iw-utils-reverse.text:
Beginning of packed resources: 37,888 (dec)

The packed files header is a simple string padded by spaces (0x20(hex)) where the first value of '504' is the number of files packed into the extender, the second number '1007' is currently unknown while the third number '10137' is the length of the file list in bytes.

String literals are escaped with 0x0A(hex) which is the line feed code or '\n' control character.

It seems that the first string starting at 38,400(dec) is "inner" and is a stand alone string and not an actual "lst" entry.  The list entries seem to actually begin directly after, and are of the format:
`<size in bytes> <file name>\n`
Where the 'line' has significant amounts of padding, seemingly for alignment either in memory or in the text file editor IW's developers used.

It appears the header, file list and each file are aligned somehow in the extender file, it is unclear what alignment is being used, as the final padding looks almost arbitrary.  This leaves significant amounts of trailing 0x00 padding between sections with no clear way to determine how much of it there really is, which inhibits our ability to extract the DOS version of the game files.

---

0x2E (ASCII 46 for periods) is used in file path strings for '..' (next directory up). However it seems also to be used for something else, like a separator between menu strings where it has three instances instead of two (see offset 0x76b38).

Another interesting note is what appears to be a variable called "g_ptrs". This may be an array or some object that holds pointers to various other game objects. It is shown in inner.exe.lst as "g_ptrs.bin" and after that at hex 0x76ea4, directly after a list of map files. Afterwards, g_ptrs is separated by blank spaces and several 4-digit hex values (the pattern is broken by a six-digit value further down) separated by several spaces as well. These may be offsets (don't appear to be sizes as they don't match with inner.exe.lst) from the starting position of g_ptrs to somewhere else in the file where these map files are stored.

---

## Data formats
Known data formats so far:

 - LBM [Interleaved Bitmap] (image file) - Internally these are stored as ".bin"
 - MOD [ProTracker module] (music file)
 - LST - List of all files included in the executable
 - CFG - Text document the executable reads and writes from for game configuration
 - SAV - Inner Worlds save file format; this and the configuration file are the only files that the executable writes out to

File format guesses:

- ITF Perhaps an internal text format, with formatting or control indicators such as '\f1' and '\c'. Probably not related to [SAPScript Interchange Text Format]
- MMP [Truevision Bravado Board Video Output format] (animation format) - There is very little documentation of the format but IW may use this as a video format for whatever reason (this is the only reasonably fitting format found on the internet so far)
- REC [?] - Appears to be an audio format associated with the MMP files as it includes the same file name as the .mmp; however this could also be the video format and the MMP is the audio
- MAP [internal map/level format]
- EOL - "End of level" - its specific purpose is currently unknown

Unknown formats:

 - RM5 - There is only one of these, "castle.rm5"
 - DUMP - A data dump of some sort but as of yet unknown as to its purpose
 - [audio] - stored internally as ".bin" and are raw waveforms stored as 8-bit signed PCM Uncompressed Mono; appear to be prefixed with s_*
 - [font] - unknown, but probably an internal font format, presumably stored in "fonts.bin" (defines the actual font data?) and "g_fonts2.bin" (the bitmap data for the font)
 - others? - To be seen after browsing file offsets from the .lst file

---

### Known file directories within the exectuable

 - ../game/
 - ../game/inner/
 - ../game/inner/e1
 - ../game/inner/e2
 - ../game/inner/e3
 - ../list/
 - root directory? (/sleepy/? see below)
 - directory commands are called from (hence '..')

#### Other miscellaneous directories (probably not useful)

 - /dev/mem (Linux physical memory file)
 - /home/baford/include/sleepy/list (this is one of the developers' Linux home directories, unknown as to why it was included in the file)

---

### Notes on original development
The game itself was written in C++ with libc5 and compiled with G++ 2.7.2 and BinUtils 2.6 into DOS and Linux executables. The developers used a custom-built DOS extender called MOSS (available at the University of Utah website) which uses a form of ELF executables and allows the main executable and any other resource files to be attached to it.

kylofon-jetstrike-sdl3-jsport-porting-md.text:
# jsport: JetStrike SDL3 port

C port of `JS_CDROM.EXE` (JetStrike CD, 1994; Watcom C, DOS/4GW, flat 32-bit) on SDL3. The original
data is read at runtime from the game folder (`Game/`, not in the repository). Specs: `../port/spec/`,
formats: `../FORMATS.md` and `../port/formats/`, bug policy: `../port/QUIRKS.md` (every original bug is kept).

Status: phase 5 step D. `main` (0x146f4) runs the real front end (step A) and the mission (step B: `Mission_Setup`, the
frame loop of `Game_Run` in its original order (`Mission_Run`, frame.c), flight model, `Player_Update`, landing / ditching /
crash / ejection, HUD, MP2 triggers, objectives, terrain damage, engine sound, `WeaponSelect_Screen`). Step C added the
weapons (weapons.c: every fire kind, the gun, projectiles, flares, explosions, particles, recon photo pages). Step D
completes the mission: enemy aircraft (spawn, movement, AI, guns, missiles, bombing, kill scoring and bonus), enemy
missiles (with the flare decoy), ground gunships, enemy shells, ejected pilots, convoys (Enemy_SetupSpriteIds,
Truck_LoadSpx), the MP2 gun / flak / SAM emplacements, target-zone vehicles, commandos, the emplacement under
construction, the airbase (fuel truck, jeep, fire engine, rearm truck -> WeaponSelect_Screen, crew, runway repair, base-hit
losses), the bonus crate with its twelve handlers, the prize balloon, the alien abduction (enemies.c) and the support
aircraft (support.c: tow plane, Fat Albert, B52, ship, big bomber, ground pickup; Tanker_Update with refuelling). No stub
of the original is left: every function the frame loop calls is ported.

## Build

Same toolchain as `srport`: MSYS2 MinGW-w64 (gcc, ninja, cmake) with SDL3 from
`C:/msys64/mingw64/lib/cmake/SDL3` (`find_package(SDL3 CONFIG)`).

```
export PATH=/c/msys64/mingw64/bin:$PATH
cmake -S jsport -B jsport/build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=gcc -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build jsport/build
```

The build copies `SDL3.dll` and what it loads (`libiconv-2.dll`, ...) next to `jsport.exe`
(`cmake/copy_dlls.cmake`). Warnings: `-Wall -Wextra` must stay clean.

## Run

```
jsport/build/jsport.exe [--game-dir DIR] [--scale N] [--fullscreen] [--sb-rate 19920|3906] [--no-intro] [--lzw-dump OUTDIR]
```

| option | meaning |
|---|---|
| `--game-dir` | the original game folder (default `Game`); CD tracks in `DIR/MUSIC/TRACKnn.WAV` (`tools/cdrip.py`) |
| `--scale` | window size 320x240 x N (default 3); Alt+Enter toggles full screen |
| `--sb-rate` | Sound Blaster mixer rate: 19920 Hz as designed (default), 3906 = the rate the original actually programs (sound.md Q1); the intro's mixer: 40000 Hz / 3906 |
| `--no-intro` | PORT: skip the intro (INTRO.EXE, which JS.BAT runs before the game; the port runs it first by default) |
| `--lzw-dump` | developer check, see Verification |

## Source layout (`src/`)

| file | content |
|---|---|
| `main.c` | options, `--lzw-dump`, start-up |
| `dseg.c/.h` | the data-segment images: LE object 5 of `JS_CDROM.EXE` loaded at start-up, `D8/D16/D32/DS32/DSTR(addr)` accessors; LE object 6 of `INTRO/INTRO.EXE` (`Iseg_Load`, `I8/I32/IS32/ISTR`) for the intro |
| `intro.c/.h` | intro.md: INTRO.EXE (`Intro_Run` from `main` before the game, as JS.BAT): its mode-X / SB mixer / CD copies, scenes, FRAME overlay, credits; exits on Esc / D release only |
| `game.h`, `game_flow.c` | game_flow.md: `Game_Run`, menus, zones, save/load, briefing, plane select, debrief, end game |
| `level.c/.h` | level.md subset: map buffers, `Map_LoadMxp`, tile accessors, Bertha stamp; `Enemy_LoadSpx`, `Enemy_SetupSpriteIds` + `Truck_LoadSpx` (convoy set-up) |
| `host.c/.h`, `host_int.h` | host layer API, init / shutdown, event pump, case-insensitive file lookup, fatal errors |
| `host_timer.c` | virtual VGA retrace clock, 59.94 Hz (25.175 MHz / 800 / 525) |
| `host_video.c` | window, 320x240 presentation (4:3, square pixels), PNG snapshots |
| `host_input.c` | SDL keys -> set-1 scancode bytes (E0 prefixes, focus loss releases), scripted keys, mouse, gamepad |
| `host_audio.c` | SDL audio device: Sound Blaster mixer stream (u8 mono, pulled), CD music stream, WAV dump |
| `platform.c/.h` | `js_main` (= `main` 0x146f4), FatalError, JS.CFG, Kbd_ISR + key slots, input (ReadControls, PollMenu, WaitKey_*, GetFKey), joystick on the SDL gamepad, Watcom `rand` / `Rand`, helpers (platform.md) |
| `files.c/.h` | `Platform_Fopen` (DOS 8.3 truncation + case-insensitive open), `File_LoadWhole` |
| `lzw.c/.h` | `LZW_Unpack` 0x50000 (LE object 2), byte-identical to `tools/jsunpack.py` |
| `mission.h` | mission globals (player, level objects, HUD, engine) as named image macros; prototypes of the mission files |
| `frame.c` | game_flow.md §8: `Mission_Run` = the frame loop of `Game_Run` (93 steps in order, flight model of player.md §3 inlined), `Fog_Refresh` |
| `player.c` | player.md: tables, controls, `Player_Update`, glider, takeoff assist, ditching, engine fire, damage, ejection, sprite helpers, crash debris |
| `hud.c` | player.md §10: `Hud_DrawPanel`, messages, radar, target arrow, briefing overlay, lamps |

New subsystems get their own files (`level.c`, `player.c`, `weapons.c`, `enemies.c`, `hud.c`, `intro.c`, ...),
one per spec, with a header for the API other files use.

## Conventions

* **One C function per original function**, same name as in `port/js_symbols.csv`, preceded by a
  `/* 0xADDR Name */` comment (plus a one-line summary if useful). Same argument order and meaning; types
  as the spec gives them (`u8/s16/u32...` from `types.h`). Functions that are inlined in the original stay
  static helpers with a comment naming where they come from.
* **Globals**: plain C globals with the original's name (`g_Palette`, `g_KeyDown`), declared in the
  subsystem header with the address in a comment (`/* 0x82ED8 */`). Initial values as in the exe's data
  object. Structs that the original reads as raw memory get `#pragma pack(1)` and the original layout.
* **`/* PORT: ... */`** marks every deviation from the original: hardware replaced (ports, IRQs, DMA,
  MSCDEX), host-crash protection, things dropped (CD check, benchmark). Behaviour that is a bug of the
  original is **not** fixed (QUIRKS.md); it gets a comment naming the quirk.
* **Host crashes**: where the original would fault (divide by zero, NULL `FILE*`, writes outside memory),
  the port stops through `FatalError` / `host_fatal_code` with a message naming the original's failure
  (e.g. `Rand(-1)`, the mixer's rate divide). Writes outside VRAM are dropped (`vput`), as on the PC.
* **Timing**: every wait of the original is a retrace wait (`Video_WaitVSync`, `Video_SetStartAndPan`);
  `host_wait_vretrace` presents the frame, pumps events and sleeps to the next 59.94 Hz boundary. The CPU
  benchmark is not run: `g_VSyncWaits = 2` (logic at 19.98 Hz, platform.md §6.4). Nothing else paces the game.
* **Keyboard**: the host delivers set-1 bytes to `Kbd_ISR` (E0 prefixes included; the ISR ignores them as
  the original does). The PC keyboard's typematic repeat is emulated (host_input.c: the last key pressed resends its
  make code after 500 ms, 30 per second, on the JS_KEYS clock); SDL's repeat events are ignored. It is not optional:
  Player_Update clears the direction slots while looking around (KP*), the repeat brings them back (platform.md
  Corrections 3). Keypad keys map by SDL scancode (position), so NumLock does not matter, as on DOS.
* **Files**: all game files go through `Platform_Fopen` / `File_LoadWhole` with the original's DOS names
  (`"data/jetstrike.spx"` opens `DATA/JETSTRIK.SPX`).
* **Sound**: the mixer runs on SDL's audio thread (`Mixer_Render`, sound.md §2.14); game-thread changes of
  `g_MixChan` go through `host_audio_lock/unlock` (inside `Mixer_SetChannel` etc.).
* **RNG**: `Rand` / `rand_js` / `srand_js` reproduce the Watcom LCG; keep every `Rand` call of the original,
  in order, including the ones whose result is unused.

## Data-segment image

Every non-pointer global of the original lives in `g_dseg`, a byte array that is LE object 5 of
`JS_CDROM.EXE` (0x80000-0x94750), read from the game folder at start-up by `Dseg_Load` (dseg.c: page map
and the internal fixups of the data object, the same logic as `tools/lefile.py`). Initial values, string
constants, tables and the layout are therefore the exe's own, and the original's out-of-bounds reads and
writes (sprite queue entry 256 over `g_Palette`, a JS.CFG key word > 0xff past `g_KeyDown`, `fgets(0x50)` into
0x28-byte name slots, the debrief `strncpy` without terminator, ...) hit the same neighbours.

```c
#define g_Mission   DS32(0x903E0)               /* named globals: a macro on their address (game.h, ...) */
DS32(0x90A08) = -1;                             /* unnamed ones in place, with the spec's address */
fopen(DSTR(0x80EE6), DSTR(0x80C77));            /* strings of the exe: "js.cfg", "rb" */
#define g_SmallCharset ((const char *)DSEG_PTR(D32(0x80011)))   /* a pointer stored in the image */
```

* Pointer-valued globals (malloc'd buffers: `g_PackBuf`, `g_MapGrid`, fonts, the sprite table
  `g_SpriteTab`, ...) stay C pointers outside the image (the image holds 32-bit DOS/4GW addresses). The sprite
  queue keeps the sprite table index where the original stored the header pointer.
* 0x1000 zero bytes follow the image (`DSEG_SLACK`); writes computed past that are dropped.
* `JS_CDROM.EXE` must be the CD version (object layout and a charset fixup are checked).
* GCC's `-Wrestrict` / `-Wstringop-truncation` are off: copies between two globals are copies inside one
  array, and `strncpy` is used as the original does.

## Developer aids (environment variables)

| variable | effect |
|---|---|
| `SDL_VIDEO_DRIVER=dummy`, `SDL_AUDIO_DRIVER=dummy` | headless run (no window, no sound device; timing unchanged) |
| `JS_SNAPSHOT_DIR=dir` | every presented frame >= `JS_SNAPSHOT_MS` (default 2000) ms after the previous one is saved as `dir/snapNNNN.png` |
| `JS_KEYS="<sec>:<xx>[+<xx>...][p\|r],..."` | scripted set-1 keys in hex at that many seconds after start (grey keys `e048`); a tap is held 0.2 s; `p` = press only, `r` = release only: `"2:39,5:01"` = Space at 2 s, Esc at 5 s; `"4:e048p,9:e048r"` holds Up for 5 s |
| `JS_QUIT_AFTER=sec` | exit after that many seconds |
| `JS_AUDIO_DUMP=file.wav` | record the mixer output (u8 mono at the SB rate) |
| `JS_SEED=n` | replaces `time(NULL)` in MainMenu's `srand` (reproducible runs) |
| `JS_VCLOCK=1` | JS_KEYS and JS_QUIT_AFTER count game time (retraces consumed x 1/59.94 s) instead of wall time, so scripted flights stay frame-exact when the host is slower than real time (PNG snapshots, traces) |
| `JS_MISSION=n` | the campaign (COMBAT) starts at mission record n of DATA/M0 (0-based); a record without a map name gets the map of the nearest earlier record preset as the loaded map |
| `JS_SFX_TRACE=1` | prints every `Sfx_Play(id, freq, vol)` call to stdout |
| `JS_TRACE=n` | prints the base / plane stats once and, every n mission frames, the player state and a line with the enemy counts (aircraft 0 position / damage, ground units, missiles, shells, convoy, vehicles, flares, bonus, score, kills, armour, engine fire, lock target, convoy vehicle 0) to stdout |

Headless example (from the repository root):

```
SDL_VIDEO_DRIVER=dummy SDL_AUDIO_DRIVER=dummy JS_SNAPSHOT_DIR=work/snap JS_SNAPSHOT_MS=1000 \
JS_KEYS="1.5:39,3:01" JS_AUDIO_DUMP=work/snap/mix.wav jsport/build/jsport.exe --game-dir Game
```

## Verification

* `python tools/lzw_check.py` runs `jsport --lzw-dump work/lzw_c` and compares every PAX/SPX/TLX/MXP/DX0/DX1
  file with `tools/jsunpack.py`: 187 files, all byte-identical (2026-10-02).
* Headless snapshots of the front end equal the decoded pictures (`tools/jsgfx.py all` -> `work/gfx/`) pixel
  for pixel apart from the text / sprites drawn over them: main menu (MISCON, rows 0..19 black, picture from
  row 20), story (COMBATCO), briefing (JETLOGO + the colour-2 underline), plane select (PLANECH + icons),
  end game (ENDGAME3, exact).
* Scripted walks (JS_KEYS, step A): campaign (story, briefing, plane select, crash debrief + end game,
  back to the menu), training, practice, load game (slot
  missing), Aerolympics options / briefing / plane select / player rotation, quit (credits printed).
* Missions (step B, JS_KEYS + JS_TRACE + snapshots): campaign mission 1 take-off ('0' full throttle, Down to
  rotate), climb, half loop (turn to the right), hop and landing to a stop on the runway, running off the runway
  end / diving into the sea (crash, damage messages, auto-eject, parachute, debrief), training LANDING (autothrottle)
  and NIGHT (night backdrop), F12 weapon select (pick a weapon, DONE, HUD redrawn). Engine loop audible in
  `JS_AUDIO_DUMP`, pitch rising with the throttle.
* Weapons (step C, JS_KEYS + JS_SEED=1 + snapshots + JS_SFX_TRACE): training BOMBING (gun bursts: ammo count, tracers,
  sfx 17 per frame; bombs: release sfx 5, pairs of bombs, explosions with fire / smoke particles and sfx 4/27 + 6,
  craters and tile replacement on the hill, score), rockets (sfx 8, pairs), Hellfire (one per press), cluster bomb (6
  bomblets, chain of explosions), JP233 / Porcupine dispensers (sfx 2 per even frame), flares (sprite 0xa0 behind the
  plane), drop tank / commando / flamer pod without faults, flying into the hill (crash particles, debris, auto-eject);
  campaign mission 1 hop with a camera pod: photo in the air, landing to a stop on the runway -> "RECON PHOTO 1" overview
  page, Space returns to the mission.
* Enemies / support aircraft (step D, JS_VCLOCK=1 + JS_SEED + JS_MISSION + JS_TRACE + snapshots + JS_SFX_TRACE):
  campaign record 10 (Junglemap2: one bomber with 2 bombs, enemy airbase, SAM-launching target vehicles): the bomber flies
  to raid the base, turns on the player, locks on, fires its gun (voice sfx 16/26) and missiles (armour hits); the player's
  automatic flare is released; target vehicles fire shells and SAMs; shooting the bomber down with the gun: explosion,
  `g_Kills` 1, +1000, "ENEMY AIRCRAFT SCRAMBLING" from the enemy base; record 2 (mission 3, the train convoy): strafing
  one car destroys the train (+3 x 250, objective cleared), landing on the runway to a stop -> "MISSION COMPLETED",
  jeep drives to the plane -> mission 4 briefing; record 0 (mission 1): Down held while parked -> the rearm truck drives to
  the plane, sfx 24 and WeaponSelect_Screen open through Airbase_Update; the tanker and the airbase vehicles / crew are
  drawn on the runway.
* `JS_AUDIO_DUMP` with Space at 1.5 s: one 0.95 s burst = 18989 samples at 19920 Hz (slice 5, `Sfx_Play(6, 12000, 0x20)`, shift 5).

## Not ported / PORT decisions so far

* Enemies (PORT): the enemy aircraft gun tracer divides by `abs(PY - y)` / `abs(PX - x)` (enemies.md Q4): kept, the port
  stops with a FatalError where the original takes a DOS/4GW divide exception. The shell dots (Q13) go to absolute VRAM as
  in the original, in colour 0xff (the original's colour byte is an unpushed stack byte). The target vehicles'
  `Video_ReadPixel` page argument is not pushed in the original: the port passes the back page. BaseHit_Losses' uninitialised
  `s` (Q21) keeps its previous value (static, starts 0).
* Weapons (PORT): the secondary-explosion arrays are bounded to 32 entries in `Explosion_Damage` as in `Map_CraterAt`;
  a bullet left of column 0 reads height 0 (the original reads the heap before the table); `Mission_CompleteScreen`
  reads MP2 column < 0 as empty and pumps events in its input waits.
* Pause and the weapon-select fire-release waits pump events (`Platform_Spin`).
* Busy loops on key memory (menu fire release, `Input_AnyKey`, `Input_GetFKey`) call `Platform_Spin`
  (events, present, 0.5 ms sleep).
* Joystick: `Joystick_Poll` reads the first SDL gamepad and places the counts around the JS.CFG thresholds;
  with the joystick off in JS.CFG (the shipped file) a connected gamepad still gives direction bits and fire.
* Save slot F10 (`js_save.00:`): loading says "Save file not found!" as on DOS; saving stops with a FatalError
  where the original writes through a NULL `FILE*` (QUIRKS.md).

* CD check / MSCDEX, the 2 MB memory probe, DPMI, INT 8 / INT 9 vectors, `Video_BenchmarkSpeed`.
* Sound Blaster: detection, DMA ring, IRQ, the 50 Hz chunk throttle (sound.md §2.13); the mono mixer
  formula is exact. GUS path not ported.
* `Sound_StopAll` clears the channels (the one stray byte per channel, Q11, is dropped).

ncmp:
        push    si
        push    di
.l:
        cmp     di, [w4]
        jae     .nz
        mov     al, [es:di]
        cmp     al, 'a'
        jb      .u
        cmp     al, 'z'
        ja      .u
        sub     al, 20h
.u:
        cmp     al, [si]
        jne     .x
        inc     si
        inc     di
        test    al, al
        jnz     .l
        jmp     .x
.nz:
        or      al, 1
.x:
        pop     di
        pop     si
        ret

        mov     si, ax
        mov     ax, [cs:qseg]
        add     ax, [w3]
        mov     es, ax
.n:

        ret
.no:

        ret

        mov     word [es:0BEh], qbsvc

        mov     word [es:0C2h], qbsvc

        mov     al, bh

        daa
        adc     al, 0x40
        daa
        mov     dl, al
        mov     ah, 2

        jnz     .l
        pop     dx

        push    ax
        push    bx
        push    cx
        push    dx
        push    si
        xor     bx, bx
        mov     cx, 10

        mov     si, ax

        mov     dx, si
        mov     si, ax
        or      si, dx
        jnz     .a

        pop     dx
        add     dl, '0'
        mov     ah, 2
        int     21h
        dec     bx
        jnz     .b
        pop     si
        pop     dx

        pop     bx
